title: A House for the Choir
premise: Petra Coldharbour hosts a small-town overnight radio show, and for seven years the dead have been calling in—voices of neighbors who died days earlier, asking her to pass on their unfinished words. She has rationalized every anomaly, but when her own sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions she never asked aloud, Petra learns the calls are not hauntings but a summons: the town's founders bound a choir of the dead beneath the old well, and the ritual that keeps them contained was left half-finished. As the well begins to refill and the choir's hunger spreads through the living town, Petra discovers she is the last heir of the founders' bloodline—chosen for invisibility so she could survive long enough to finish what they started. In the flooded dark beneath the well, she must choose between completing the ritual and freeing the choir, and her choice rewrites what inheritance means: she gives the dead their voices back by taking them into her own.
about_author: Orsen Reyes is a former late-night radio engineer who spent a decade in stations he swears were haunted, collecting the stories of insomniac callers. He writes horror about quiet people who inherit loud obligations, and lives somewhere with very good reception.

chapters.title: Dead Air
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. During her overnight show, a caller asks Petra to tell his daughter he forgave her—then Petra finds his obituary dated four days ago. She logs it as another coincidence, but her hands shake through the rest of the shift. Emotional beat: dread disguised as routine; the reader sees how much Petra explains away.

chapters.title: The Sleep Tapes
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Reviewing recordings made to diagnose her insomnia, Petra hears herself ask questions in her sleep—and hears a second voice, low and choral, answering. The voice knows things only the dead callers knew. Emotional beat: the collapse of her seven-year architecture of denial.

chapters.title: Callers
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. She tests the show deliberately, reading out names from old obituaries; the phone lines light up with voices matching each name. A caller warns her: 'Stop digging before the well refills.' Emotional beat: vertigo—the phenomenon responds to her attention.

chapters.title: Coldharbour Ground
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Researching her family name at the county archive, she learns the Coldharbours were among the town's founders and owned the land around the dry well on the hill. Every record after 1911 is water-damaged. Emotional beat: inheritance as something buried, literally.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Names Her
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. On air, the second voice breaks through the broadcast itself, addressing Petra by a childhood nickname no living person uses. Listeners call in terrified; her producer hears nothing on the master tape. Emotional beat: isolation—only Petra can witness this.

chapters.title: Marta Vane
chapters.summary: Marta's POV. An elderly archivist who has waited decades for a Coldharbour to come asking questions, Marta reveals the founders' covenant: they drowned a chorus of wronged townsfolk in the well to silence testimony of a massacre, then built a ritual to keep the dead singing instead of speaking. Emotional beat: the town's justice was an erasure.

chapters.title: Half a Ritual
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Marta shows her the founders' ledger: the binding rite has seven movements, and the founders completed only five before dying or fleeing. The sixth requires 'the heir who was kept invisible.' Petra realizes her parents' secrecy was preparation. Emotional beat: fury at a life engineered without consent.

chapters.title: What the Well Wants
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Water begins seeping into the dry well ahead of any rain. Around town, mirrors fog with breath-prints, and the recently bereaved report hearing full choirs under their floors. Emotional beat: escalation—the containment is failing and the deadline is real.

chapters.title: The Caller Who Wasn't Dead Yet
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. A woman calls the show begging for help, then dies mid-sentence; minutes later she calls again from the other side, describing the well's interior—a flooded chamber lined with mouths. Emotional beat: horror sharpened by intimacy; Petra spoke with her while she drowned.

chapters.title: Invisible by Design
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, with flashbacks. Petra excavates memories: moved towns, erased records, a mother who taught her to be unremarkable like a survival skill. She confronts her estranged father by phone; he hangs up on the word 'well.' Emotional beat: grief for a self that was amputated to fit a prophecy.

chapters.title: Sixth Movement
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Deciphering the ledger's sixth movement, she learns it demands the heir speak the names of the drowned aloud at the wellhead—restoring identity before release. But the seventh movement's page is torn out. Emotional beat: hope with a hole in it.

chapters.title: The Choir Surfaces
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. The well overflows its shaft; black water moves uphill through storm drains. The choir possesses the town's PA system during the harvest festival, singing the massacre victims' names until listeners weep without knowing why. Emotional beat: the dead demanding recognition at civic scale.

chapters.title: Vigilantes of the Living
chapters.summary: Deputy Aris Kell's POV. Town councilmen, descendants of the massacre's perpetrators, plan to seal the well with concrete and silence Petra permanently. Aris, whose own grandfather's name is in the ledger, defects and warns her. Emotional beat: justice outside the law—some inheritances must be refused.

chapters.title: They Come for the Station
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Councilmen torch the radio station mid-broadcast; Petra escapes through the transmitter room as the choir's voices shield her, guiding her past the smoke. The station burns; the signal does not stop. Emotional beat: terror transmuting into resolve—she cannot be silenced because she carries the dead now.

chapters.title: The Torn Page
chapters.summary: Aris and Petra's shared POV. Following Marta's clues to the founders' crypt, they find the seventh movement sewn into a founder's burial shroud: the ritual ends with the heir taking the choir into themselves—becoming the vessel, the house for the choir. Emotional beat: the cost named at last.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra attempts a shortcut—naming the dead at the wellhead without accepting the seventh movement. The ritual stalls; the choir's anguish cracks windows across town, and Marta dies at her archive desk with a hymn on her lips. Emotional beat: failure and the lesson that half-measures are the founders' original sin.

chapters.title: Descent
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. With the well nearly full and the town evacuating, Petra goes down the shaft with Aris holding the rope, carrying the ledger and a recorder—her radio voice as her weapon and offering. Emotional beat: chosen courage; she stops being invisible by walking toward the thing she feared.

chapters.title: The Flooded Chamber
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Beneath the waterline she meets the choir face to face: the massacred townsfolk, still waiting to testify. They do not want vengeance; they want to be heard, named, remembered. The founders' crime was making them sing instead of speak. Emotional beat: compassion inside horror.

chapters.title: Seventh Movement
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra speaks all one hundred and twelve names, then opens herself as the vessel—the choir pours into her, and she broadcasts their testimony through every speaker in the county as the well drains. The truth of the massacre plays over the town at last. Emotional beat: climax; justice achieved not by law but by witness.

chapters.title: After the Signal
chapters.summary: Aris's POV. The councilmen are arrested on evidence the broadcast made undeniable; the town holds a memorial where the festival once drowned in song. Aris pulls Petra from the empty well, barely alive, her voice changed—layered, harmonic. Emotional beat: exhaustion, accountability, dawn.

chapters.title: A House for the Choir
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Recovering, Petra accepts that the choir remains within her—not as possession but as company, the dead finally housed rather than hidden. She rebuilds the station as a low-power community frequency where the town tells its true history aloud. Emotional beat: inheritance reclaimed as stewardship.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Petra's POV, final broadcast. On the anniversary night, Petra hosts one last show, letting the choir harmonize beneath her words as she reads the names again for anyone newly arrived in town. When she signs off, the second voice says, softly, 'Goodnight, Petra'—and for the first time it sounds like gratitude. Emotional beat: peace; the noises finally have an explanation, and it is hers.
